hints: Focus on whether each reaction is a harsh industrial or heated lab preparation, or a quick qualitative test you do in a test tube on the bench.
Recall the conditions for cracking of alkanes and for making amines from halogenoalkanes, both need strong heating, and that $\text{KBr}$ alone cannot convert an alcohol to a bromoalkane.
Think about what the 2,4-DNPH test for aldehydes and ketones looks like in practice and whether you need to heat it to get the orange precipitate.
walkthrough:
**Sort reactions by conditions needed**

Think like a practical chemist. Some organic reactions have high activation energy and need strong heat. Others are fast addition or condensation tests that work on the bench at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Rule to use:
$$\text{rate depends on } E_a \text{ and conditions, qualitative tests are designed to be fast at room temperature}$$

**Check A, B and C for heating**

Reaction A is cracking of decane. This needs very high temperature ($600$ to $700^{\circ}\text{C}$) and a catalyst. Reaction B is nucleophilic substitution to make an amine. This needs heating in a sealed tube with excess ethanolic $\text{NH}_3$. Reaction C as written does not even happen. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{KBr}$ will not give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$. You need $\text{HBr}$ made from $\text{KBr} +$ concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ plus heat.

**Confirm the 2,4-DNPH reaction**

Reaction D is the classic test for a carbonyl group:
$$ (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CO} + \text{H}_2\text{NNHC}_6\text{H}_3(\text{NO}_2)_2 \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=NNHC}_6\text{H}_3(\text{NO}_2)_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} $$
This is nucleophilic addition-elimination of propanone to form an orange 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. It happens quickly on shaking at room temperature with no heating, so this is the answer.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22} \rightarrow \text{C}_8\text{H}_{18} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ is catalytic cracking. Breaking strong C-C bonds needs a very high activation energy, so temperatures of several hundred degrees plus a catalyst are required, not $20^{\circ}\text{C}$.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NH}_3$ is nucleophilic substitution to form a primary amine. In the lab this is heated in a sealed tube with excess ammonia in ethanol. At room temperature it is far too slow to be a good rate.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{KBr}$ does not react as written. $\text{Br}^-$ is a weak nucleophile and $\text{OH}^-$ is a poor leaving group. To make a bromoalkane you need to generate $\text{HBr}$ in situ and heat, so this fails on both feasibility and conditions.
options.D: Correct. This is the 2,4-DNPH test for aldehydes and ketones. Propanone undergoes condensation with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine to give the orange hydrazone plus water. It is designed as a rapid qualitative test and gives a precipitate at a good rate at room temperature.
